:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=e^x\sin x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\dfrac \pi 2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^x$ and $v(x)=\sin{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = e^x,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+sin⁡x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\dfrac\pi 2$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi /2} & ={e}^{\pi /2}(cos⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+sin⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e^{\pi/2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y = 2e^{x}(x + 1)$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x = 0$.
If a curve $C$ is given by $y = 8x^{3}\sin x$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x = \frac{π}{2}$.
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=3{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{tan}x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(3{x}^{2})({sec}^{2}x)+(\operatorname{tan}x)(6x) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}x+6x\operatorname{tan}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=\pi } & =3{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}x+6x\operatorname{tan}x{|}_{x=\pi } \\  & =3(\pi )^{2}{sec}^{2}(\pi )+6(\pi )\operatorname{tan}(\pi ) \\  & =3{\pi }^{2}\cdot 1+6\pi \cdot 0 \\  & =3{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $3{\pi }^{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(x-1)\operatorname{ln}(2x+1),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x-1$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}(2x+1).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{2x+1}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x-1)\cdot \frac{2}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2(x-1)}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & =\frac{2(0-1)}{2(0)+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2(0)+1) \\  & =(-2)+\operatorname{ln}(1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-2.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
If a curve $C$ is defined by the equation $y=f(x)\cdot h(x),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$

Slope $\,=${{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(x+2)cos⁡x,$ then the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is{{field-1}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x+2$ and $v(x)=cos⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-sin⁡x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x+2)\cdot (-sin⁡x)+cos⁡x\cdot 1 \\  & =-(x+2)sin⁡x+cos⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\frac{\pi }{2}} & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)sin⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+cos⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)(1)+0 \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-\frac{\pi }{2}-2.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(x-1)ln⁡(4x-3),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is{{field-1}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x-1$ and $v(x)=ln⁡(4x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4}{4x-3}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x-1)\cdot \frac{4}{4x-3}+ln⁡(4x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=1$ into the formula and get

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=({x}^{2}-4x+7){e}^{x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.

$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =({x}^{2}-4x+7)\cdot {e}^{x}+{e}^{x}\cdot (2x-4) \\  & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-2x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(3x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1.$

$$

$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(3x-2)\cdot \frac{1}{x}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{3x-2}{x}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=\cos x .$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	 (x\cos x)' &=   u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\\
						&= (x)'\cdot \cos x + x\cdot (\cos x)'\\
					   & = 1 \cdot \cos x + x (-\sin x)\\
					  & =  \cos x - x \sin x					

\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we have the two functions $u(x)=2x^3$ and $v(x)=x^2.$ How do we calculate the derivative of their product $(u(x) \cdot v(x))'?$

To do that, we can use the **product rule**, which states that the derivative of the product of two functions is given by the formula

$$
\left(u(x) \cdot  v(x)\right)' = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x).
$$

In our case, the derivatives of the two functions are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =(2{x}^{3})^{′}=6{x}^{2}, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2})^{′}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug all of this into the product rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{′} & =(6{x}^{2})({x}^{2})+(2{x}^{3})(2x) \\  & =6{x}^{4}+4{x}^{4} \\  & =10{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

This example was quite simple, and we could have solved it by calculating the product first and then taking the derivative. We can do it now to double check our result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{′} & =(2{x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})^{′} \\  & =(2{x}^{5})^{′} \\  & =10{x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we cannot calculate the product algebraically, or it can be tedious to do it. In those cases, the product rule will turn out to be very useful!

$$
\begin{aligned}
	 (x\cos x)' &=   u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\\
						&= (x)'\cdot \cos x + x\cdot (\cos x)'\\
					   & = 1 \cdot \cos x + x (-\sin x)\\
					  & =  \cos x - x \sin x					

\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Product Containing a Trigonometric Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = x^2$ and $v(x)=\ln x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2})}^{′}ln⁡x+{x}^{2}{(ln⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =2x\cdot ln⁡x+{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =2xln⁡x+x \\  & =x(2ln⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Product Containing an Exponential or Logarithmic Function

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The product rule can also be written using *Leibniz notation*:

If $y = u(x) \cdot v(x),$ then 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} \cdot  v + u \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=e^x\sin x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\dfrac \pi 2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^x$ and $v(x)=\sin{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = e^x,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+sin⁡x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\dfrac\pi 2$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi /2} & ={e}^{\pi /2}(cos⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+sin⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e^{\pi/2}.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y=3x^2+1$ where the tangent line has a slope of $-1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+1.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to $f'(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+1) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =3\cdot 2x+0 \\  & =6x+0 \\  & =6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set $f'(x) = -1$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-1 \\ 6x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $-1$ at the point where $x=-\dfrac 1 6.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Point on a Curve With a Certain Slope

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + \dfrac {1}{x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^2+\dfrac 1 x.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to $f'(2).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =2\cdot x-{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =2(2)-(2{)}^{-2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\dfrac{15}{4}.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Slope of a Tangent Line of a Curve at a Given Point

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^4 + 3\sqrt [3]{x^2}$ at the point $(1,4)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
This time, we'll use $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =4\cdot {x}^{3}+3\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {x}^{-1/3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}+2{x}^{-1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =4(1{)}^{3}+2(1{)}^{-1/3} \\  & =4+2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $6.$
